strengths: Jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies addresses a useful systems problem. The ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge experiments establish relevance to training large computer vision models.

Table 1 reports meaningful measured gains. On ENVB-8, ViT-Huge reaches 45.58 samples/s versus 38.74 for Alpa and 32.20 for Galvatron; Swin-Huge reaches 19.08 versus 13.90 for Galvatron. The Llama-7B improvement on ENVC is 3.80×. Matching Galvatron's throughput on several ENVA workloads while reducing search time also has practical value.

The evaluation covers four hardware environments, including NVIDIA GPUs and Hygon DCUs, and demonstrates weak scaling to 64 DCUs. Baseline failures and unavailable implementations are disclosed, and the BERT case study explains how selected strategies exploit communication topology.

The manuscript provides optimization pseudocode, model configurations, solver settings, and a cost-model assessment reporting 3.59% average estimation error on selected strategies. These details support understanding of the proposed system.
weaknesses: The stated placement constraints permit solutions whose communication cost is incorrectly omitted. Equations (6a–c) establish contiguity but do not order pipeline stages. For a two-layer chain u→v, placing u in stage 2 and v in stage 1 satisfies the contiguity and placement constraints, yet Equation (4) assigns zero communication cost because P_u1 P_v2=0. Thus, the written optimizer can prefer a placement by dropping a real transfer. Appendix B does not resolve this issue; additional ordering constraints are needed.

The advertised MIQP formulation is incomplete. Equations (3) and (4) contain fourth-degree products of decision variables, such as P_ui P_vi S_uk S_vl. An auxiliary-variable reformulation can address this, but none is supplied. This is a correctable specification gap, rather than evidence that the approach is impossible, but it prevents reproducing the actual solver formulation central to the contribution.

The memory model does not explain GPipe's retention of activations across micro-batches. Algorithm 1 passes b=B/c to CostModeling, Section 3.2 scales activation memory by that batch size, and Equation (5) introduces no factor accounting for c retained micro-batches. With checkpointing disabled, GPipe must retain activations across the forward sweep. As written, the constraint can underestimate peak memory; the reported throughput-estimation accuracy does not validate this feasibility guarantee.

The unqualified optimality claims exceed the reported evidence. Appendix E imposes a 60-second time limit and permits early termination with a relative MIP gap below 4%, but achieved gaps and timeout frequencies are not reported. Moreover, optimization concerns an approximate cost model and a restricted enumerated strategy space. Section 3.5's polynomial runtime argument relies on capping solver time and therefore does not establish polynomial-time optimal optimization.

The ablation does not isolate the central advantage claimed over hierarchical search. Figure 6 compares combined search with inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only variants, although competing hierarchical methods already combine both categories. A comparison using a shared cost model and execution backend is absent. Since UniAP also reports more accurate cost estimates, the observed gains do not establish that joint optimization itself explains the improvement. Hierarchical decomposition alone does not imply suboptimality.

Search-time improvements require qualification: the measured UOP time excludes profiling, and Section 4.2 attributes substantial gains to multithreaded Gurobi versus single-threaded baselines without a resource-matched comparison. These are secondary limitations. My weak-reject recommendation is primarily determined by the consequential formulation and memory-accounting gaps, together with insufficient evidence for the central optimization claim, despite the worthwhile measured performance gains.
